package.title: Top 5 Funniest Fashion Fails in History
package.description:
Five funny fashion trends in history that people really wore, from giant ruffs and towering wigs to weird historical fashion like platform shoes over 18 inches tall. Number one is the pointy medieval shoes a king limited by law in 1463.

In this Short: ruff collars, panniers, macaroni wigs, chopines and poulaines.

Sources:
https://getty.edu/news/uncomfortable-shoes-of-the-middle-ages
https://getty.edu/news/uncomfortable-shoes-of-the-middle-ages
https://fashionhistory.fitnyc.edu/chopines/
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some people stuffed the toes of their pointy shoes with moss or horsehair just to keep them stiff. Which trend should make a comeback?

scenes.text: Before you laugh at your own old outfits, see the shoes an English king had to limit. Here are the five funniest fashion fails in history.
scenes.label: 5 real fashion fails
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a long pointed medieval style shoe alongside a slow pan across old portraits in a museum gallery.

scenes.text: Number five, the giant ruff. These starched collars stuck out about nine inches, like wearing a frilly dinner plate.
scenes.label: A collar like a plate
scenes.image_prompt: Portrait painting of a person in a huge white ruff collar with a stack of white dinner plates beside a lace collar.

scenes.text: Number four, panniers. These hoops made skirts so wide, some had hinges to fold up for doorways.
scenes.label: Folding skirts for doors
scenes.image_prompt: Museum mannequin in a very wide 18th century gown standing in front of a narrow old wooden doorway in a historic house.

scenes.text: Number three, macaroni wigs. Cartoonists drew these powdered wigs nearly half the wearer's size. And yes, that's the macaroni in Yankee Doodle, the fashion, not the pasta.
scenes.label: Not the pasta
scenes.image_prompt: Tall white powdered wig on a stand next to an old engraving-style drawing and a bowl of macaroni pasta.

scenes.text: Number two, chopines. These Italian platform shoes could be over eighteen inches tall.
scenes.label: Over 18 inches tall
scenes.image_prompt: Venice canal lined with old buildings and a person wearing extremely tall platform shoes.

scenes.text: Number one, poulaines, shoes with toes so long they were stuffed with moss or horsehair. In fourteen sixty-three, King Edward the Fourth limited anyone who wasn't a noble to toes of two inches. That's the shoe a king had to limit by law.
scenes.label: A shoe law. Really.
scenes.image_prompt: Pointed leather shoe tip filled with straw next to an old parchment scroll with a red wax seal and a ruler measuring the toe.

scenes.text: Which of these five would you dare to wear to school? Tell me, then go see those shoes again.
scenes.label: Back to the shoes
scenes.image_prompt: Empty school hallway with lockers transitioning to a slow pan along a long pointed shoe.

key_facts: Giant ruff collars stuck out about nine inches like a dinner plate.
Panniers were hoops that made skirts so wide they needed hinges for doorways.
Macaroni wigs were powdered wigs drawn by cartoonists nearly half the wearer's size.
The macaroni in Yankee Doodle refers to the fashion trend, not pasta.
Chopines were Italian platform shoes over eighteen inches tall.
Poulaines were medieval shoes with extremely long toes stuffed with moss or horsehair.
In 1463, King Edward the Fourth limited non-nobles to shoe toes of two inches by law.

package.title: How Mapmakers Invented a Town in 1925
package.description:
Agloe, New York was a fake town on a map, made up by mapmakers as a copyright trap to catch copycats. This is how that paper town ended up becoming real.

In this Short: the 1920s map trap, the fishing lodge that took the name, and how Agloe ended up in a US government database.

This is a true story.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agloe,_New_York
https://www.amusingplanet.com/2017/03/agloe-fake-town-that-became-real_19.html
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: fake places like Agloe are called 'paper towns', and mapmakers used them to prove someone copied their work. Would you ever visit a town that started as a trap?

scenes.text: Before you trust your map, you should know about Agloe, the town that was never supposed to exist. This is the true story of a fake town that became real.
scenes.label: True story
scenes.image_prompt: An old paper road map unfolding on a rustic wooden table under warm lighting

scenes.text: In the nineteen-twenties, two mapmakers wanted to catch copycats. So they invented a tiny town on a New York dirt road.
scenes.label: A fake dot on the map
scenes.image_prompt: A vintage drafting desk with old fountain pens, rulers, and a half-drawn map

scenes.text: They named it Agloe, from their initials. If Agloe showed up on another map, it was copied. Here's the twist.
scenes.label: The copycat trap
scenes.image_prompt: A magnifying glass sliding over a vintage map highlighting a tiny printed town name

scenes.text: Around nineteen-thirty, a nearby fishing lodge took the name for real. The story goes that Agloe later turned up on a rival company's map.
scenes.label: Agloe Lodge: real!
stock_queries: two road maps side by side
scenes.image_prompt: A rustic wooden fishing lodge beside a quiet stream in a green forest

scenes.text: The rival said the name was now in real county records. The trap caught nothing, because the fake town had turned real.
scenes.label: Real county records
scenes.image_prompt: An old metal filing cabinet filled with dusty paper records and historical documents

scenes.text: In twenty-fourteen, Agloe even landed in a US government database. So that's Agloe, the fake town people made real by believing the map.
scenes.label: In a government database
scenes.image_prompt: A computer screen scrolling through a long database list of geographical place names

scenes.text: If you could invent one fake town, what would you name it? Tell me, and next time you open a map, think of Agloe.
scenes.label: THE END
scenes.image_prompt: A hand opening a crisp folded road map outdoors against a bright sunset background

key_facts: Agloe was invented in the 1920s by two mapmakers as a copyright trap.
The name Agloe was created from the initials of the mapmakers.
Around 1930, a real fishing lodge took the name Agloe.
A rival company included Agloe on their map because it appeared in real county records.
In 2014, Agloe appeared in a US government database.
package.script: Before you trust your map, you should know about Agloe, the town that was never supposed to exist. This is the true story of a fake town that became real. In the nineteen-twenties, two mapmakers wanted to catch copycats. So they invented a tiny town on a New York dirt road. They named it Agloe, from their initials. If Agloe showed up on another map, it was copied. Here's the twist. Around nineteen-thirty, a nearby fishing lodge took the name for real. The story goes that Agloe later turned up on a rival company's map. The rival said the name was now in real county records. The trap caught nothing, because the fake town had turned real. In twenty-fourteen, Agloe even landed in a US government database. So that's Agloe, the fake town people made real by believing the map. If you could invent one fake town, what would you name it? Tell me, and next time you open a map, think of Agloe.

package.title: Why Golf Balls Have 300+ Dimples
package.description:
Why do golf balls have dimples, and how many dimples on a golf ball are there? Most have 300 to 500 golf ball dimples, and they cut drag and add lift so the ball flies about twice as far as a smooth one.

In this Short: how a smooth ball drags, what the dimples do to the air, and why beat-up balls flew farther.

Sources:
https://mentalfloss.com/article/650345/why-golf-balls-have-dimples
https://www.scienceabc.com/sports/golf-balls-dimpled-reason-speed-air-aerodynamic-drag.html

package.title: Play-Doh Was Wallpaper Cleaner for 20 Years
package.description:
Play-Doh history in under a minute: Play-Doh was a wallpaper cleaner for about 20 years before it became a toy. Here's who invented Play-Doh as a toy, and the teacher who gave it its second life.

In this Short: coal soot, Kutol's wallpaper cleaner, and how teacher Kay Zufall helped turn it into Play-Doh.

This is a true story.

Sources:
https://www.museumofplay.org/blog/the-history-of-play-doh-good-clean-fun/
https://greatpatent.com/play-doh-was-a-wallpaper-cleaner-dying-with-the-coal-furnace

package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: by 1957, just a couple of years after its toy debut, Play-Doh came in red, yellow and blue. Which color did you always grab first?

scenes.text: You've squished it, but you've never known Play-Doh started out cleaning soot off walls in Cincinnati. Here's how a wall cleaner became a famous toy.

scenes.text: In the nineteen-thirties, many homes burned coal, which left sooty grime on wallpaper. So a Cincinnati soap company called Kutol sold a doughy putty you'd roll over walls to lift the dirt.
scenes.label: 1930s coal soot
scenes.image_prompt: An old coal stove glowing in a vintage room with hands rolling a putty cleaner across patterned wallpaper

scenes.text: It was a wall cleaner for about twenty years. But after World War Two, families switched to oil and gas heat. Less soot, fewer dirty walls, and sales slid.
scenes.label: ~20 years of cleaning
scenes.image_prompt: Vintage calendar pages flipping quickly in a dimly lit room, followed by a close-up of a blue gas furnace flame

scenes.text: Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall had her class make crafts with it. She told her brother-in-law, Joe McVicker, who ran the company, to sell it as a toy.
scenes.label: Teacher Kay Zufall
scenes.image_prompt: Children in a mid-century classroom making crafts with soft clay, retro style photography

scenes.text: In the mid nineteen-fifties, it got a new name, Play-Doh. So that's the twist, the toy in your hands was made to clean walls.
scenes.label: PLAY-DOH is born
scenes.image_prompt: Vintage factory production line stacking colorful tubs of modeling dough with retro packaging

scenes.text: What's the best thing you've made out of Play-Doh? So next time you squish it, think of a sooty wall in Cincinnati.

It was a wall cleaner for about twenty years. But after World War Two, families switched to oil and gas heat. Less soot, fewer dirty walls, and sales slid. Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall had her class make crafts with it. She told her brother-in-law, Joe McVicker, who ran the company, to sell it as a toy. In the mid nineteen-fifties, it got a new name, Play-Doh. So that's the twist, the toy in your hands was made to clean walls. What's the best thing you've made out of Play-Doh? So next time you squish it, think of a sooty wall in Cincinnati.

package.title: Top 5 Animals That Play Dead Like Pros

Five animals that play dead like pros, counted down to the champion. Meet a hognose snake playing dead that flips back over, and an opossum playing dead so well it even smells the part.

In this Short: a pebble-like beetle, a peeking frog, an ambush fish, the hognose snake and the Virginia opossum.

scenes.text:
Why would an animal play dead, and which one never stops acting even when you flip it?
Here are the five best fakers in nature.
scenes.image_prompt: Cinematic macro shot of an eastern hognose snake lying belly-up on a forest floor with its tongue dangling, dramatic natural lighting.

scenes.text:
Number five, the death-feigning beetle.
It tucks in its legs and looks just like a pebble.
scenes.label: DEATH-FEIGNING BEETLE
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a small dark death-feigning beetle with legs tucked in tightly, resting among tiny pebbles on dry soil.

scenes.text:
Number four, a tiny frog from Brazil.
It flips over, shuts its eyes, then peeks to see if you're gone.
scenes.label: BRAZILIAN FROG
scenes.image_prompt: Macro photography of a tiny brown Brazilian frog lying on its back on green rainforest leaf litter, one eye slightly open peeking.

scenes.text:
Number three, Livingstone's cichlid, an African lake fish.
It lies on its side looking dead, and when small fish come close, it strikes.
scenes.label: LIVINGSTONE'S CICHLID
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater view of a colorful cichlid fish lying motionless on its side on a sandy African lake bottom, waiting to ambush.

scenes.text:
Number two, the eastern hognose snake.
It rolls over, tongue out, and if you flip it upright, it rolls right back.
scenes.label: HOGNOSE SNAKE
scenes.image_prompt: Detailed shot of an eastern hognose snake lying on its back in green grass with its mouth open and tongue sticking out.

scenes.text:
Number one, the Virginia opossum.
It goes stiff, tongue out, and even gives off a stinky smell, sometimes for hours.
And it's not even trying, it happens automatically.
So the snake never quits when flipped, but the possum wins, it even smells the part.
scenes.label: VIRGINIA OPOSSUM
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a Virginia opossum lying stiff on its side in tall grass, mouth open and eyes glazed over in fake death.

scenes.text:
Which of these would fool you best?
Next time an animal lies perfectly still, ask yourself.

package.description:
Can you do these 3 body tricks? Try the ring finger trick, the foot and number six trick, and the tongue rolling test, then find out why most body tricks you can't do aren't your fault.

package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the scientist who first called tongue rolling a simple gene later said he was embarrassed it was still in textbooks. Which trick beat you, one, two or three?

scenes.text: Can you do these three body tricks? Lots of people fail at least one, and there's a real reason why. Try each one right now.
scenes.label: Can you do them?
scenes.image_prompt: First-person POV of someone looking at their own open hands resting on a clean wooden table, cinematic lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick one. Hand flat on a table, middle finger folded under. Now lift just your ring finger.
scenes.label: Lift your ring finger
scenes.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of a human hand flat on a wooden desk with middle finger tucked under palm, trying to lift ring finger, vertical framing

scenes.text: Stuck? Little tendon bridges tie it to its neighbors, so it can't lift alone.
scenes.label: Tendon bridges
scenes.image_prompt: Anatomical visualization of human hand tendons connecting the ring finger to adjacent fingers, glowing fiber lines, dark background, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick two. Circle your right foot clockwise. Keep going, and draw a six in the air with your right hand.
scenes.label: Foot clockwise, draw a 6
scenes.image_prompt: Person sitting on a chair circling their right foot in the air while drawing the number 6 with their right index finger, split action focus, vertical framing

scenes.text: Did your foot flip? For lots of people, it does. Scientists aren't sure why, but one idea is your brain links plans for limbs on the same side.
scenes.label: Same-side brain link
scenes.image_prompt: Stylized glowing brain illustration showing neural signals firing down to the right side of the body, high-tech science aesthetic, vertical framing

scenes.text: Trick three. Roll your tongue into a U. Roughly sixty-five to eighty-one percent of people can.
scenes.label: Roll your tongue
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up portrait of a cheerful person effortlessly rolling their tongue into a U-tube shape, bright natural lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: Textbooks called it a simple gene, but identical twins don't always match.
scenes.label: Not just simple genetics
scenes.image_prompt: Side-by-side shot of identical twins where one successfully rolls their tongue and the other tries and smiles, bright studio lighting, vertical framing

scenes.text: So now you know why your finger sticks, your foot flips, and your tongue might not roll. Which trick beat you? Tell me in the comments. Now ask a friend the same thing.
scenes.label: Which trick beat you?
scenes.image_prompt: Two friends sitting across a table laughing while testing funny hand and foot tricks together, cozy modern cafe setting, vertical framing

key_facts: The ring finger cannot easily lift independently when the middle finger is bent due to connecting fibrous tendon bands (juncturae tendinum).
Circling the right foot clockwise while drawing a number six with the right hand often causes the foot to involuntarily reverse direction due to ipsilateral motor coordination in the brain.
Between 65% and 81% of people can roll their tongue into a U shape.
Tongue rolling is not governed by a single dominant gene, as evidenced by identical twins who do not always share the trait.
package.script: Can you do these three body tricks? Lots of people fail at least one, and there's a real reason why. Try each one right now. Trick one. Hand flat on a table, middle finger folded under. Now lift just your ring finger. Stuck? Little tendon bridges tie it to its neighbors, so it can't lift alone. Trick two. Circle your right foot clockwise. Keep going, and draw a six in the air with your right hand. Did your foot flip? For lots of people, it does. Scientists aren't sure why, but one idea is your brain links plans for limbs on the same side. Trick three. Roll your tongue into a U. Roughly sixty-five to eighty-one percent of people can. scenes.label: TIE!

scenes.label: NO CRUMBS

scenes.text: Fix one, check the floor. Slide the table a little and see if the wobble disappears. Often it's the floor that's uneven, not the table.

key_facts: Wobbling is frequently caused by uneven floor contours rather than flawed table legs.

A stable contact orientation occurs within a 90-degree (quarter turn) rotation.
Abrupt discontinuities like sharp tile thresholds or steps violate the theorem's continuity premise.
A rotation-stabilized table may rest at a slight incline, but rocking motion is eliminated.

scenes.text: What if I told you there's no egg and no cream in an egg cream? And that's not even the worst food name. Here are five foods with lying names.
scenes.label: NO EGG. NO CREAM.
scenes.image_prompt: A vintage American diner table showing a fizzy chocolate egg cream in a tall soda fountain glass next to an old-fashioned menu, bright cinematic lighting.

scenes.text: Number five, buffalo wings. Zero buffalo. They're chicken wings named after Buffalo, New York.
scenes.label: #5 BUFFALO WINGS
scenes.image_prompt: A steaming plate of saucy red glazed chicken wings garnished with celery, with a humorous faint silhouette of a wild American bison in the background.

scenes.text: Number four, Bombay duck. Not a duck. It's a fish, often dried and salted until it's crunchy.
scenes.label: #4 BOMBAY DUCK
scenes.image_prompt: Crisp golden fried Bombay duck fish arranged on a rustic plate, humorously accompanied by a yellow rubber duck sitting on the side.

scenes.text: Number three, Welsh rarebit. It was once called Welsh rabbit, but it's just melted cheese on toast.
scenes.label: #3 WELSH RAREBIT
scenes.image_prompt: Warm rich cheddar cheese sauce bubbling under a broiler on thick slices of crusty toasted bread, delicious food photography.

scenes.text: Number two, the egg cream. It's just chocolate syrup, milk and seltzer.
scenes.label: #2 EGG CREAM

scenes.text: So the biggest liar on the menu? Toad in the hole, with zero toads. Which food name fooled you longest? Tell me in the comments. And next time someone hands you an egg cream, ask them one question.
scenes.label: BIGGEST MENU LIAR
scenes.image_prompt: A puzzled diner customer holding a quirky restaurant menu with exaggerated question marks, surrounded by comic dishes like sausages in batter and soda drinks.

key_facts: An egg cream contains neither egg nor cream, but is made from chocolate syrup, milk, and seltzer.
Buffalo wings are chicken wings that originated in Buffalo, New York, not from buffalo meat.
Bombay duck is a species of lizardfish that is typically salted and dried, not poultry.
Welsh rarebit, originally known as Welsh rabbit, consists of savory melted cheese sauce served over toasted bread.
Toad in the hole is an English dish consisting of sausages baked into Yorkshire pudding batter, containing no actual amphibians.

scenes.text: Before you scroll, what color is the sun? Hint, it's not yellow. Three color questions, three seconds each. Lock in your answer.
scenes.label: 3 Questions, 3 Seconds
scenes.image_prompt: A brilliant white sun glowing high in a deep blue sky with subtle lens flares, sharp high-resolution photography.

scenes.text: Question one. What color is the sun, really? Three, two, one.
scenes.label: What color is the sun?
scenes.image_prompt: The sun shining brightly from space against a pitch black starry void, radiating pure white light.

scenes.text: White! Sunlight is almost pure white. Our air makes it look yellow, especially when it's low in the sky.
scenes.label: White
scenes.image_prompt: A warm golden sunset transition showing atmospheric haze scattering sunlight over a calm ocean horizon.

scenes.text: Question two. What color is a polar bear's skin? Three, two, one.
scenes.label: What color is polar bear skin?
scenes.image_prompt: A large polar bear walking across crisp white arctic snowdrifts under a bright arctic sky, realistic wildlife photo.

scenes.text: Black! Cubs are born with pink skin, and it turns black after a few months. And each hair of its fur is see-through. It just looks white.
scenes.label: Black

scenes.image_prompt: Extreme macro close-up of a polar bear showing dark black skin beneath translucent hollow white fur strands.

scenes.label: What color is a baby flamingo?
scenes.image_prompt: A fluffy grey flamingo chick standing beside the slender pink legs of its parent on a sunny wetland shore.

scenes.text: Grey! Flamingos only turn pink from pigments in the algae and tiny creatures they eat.
scenes.label: Grey
scenes.image_prompt: A flock of vibrant pink flamingos wading and feeding in shallow tropical blue water, detailed nature photography.

scenes.text: So the sun is white, the polar bear is black underneath, and baby flamingos are grey. How many did you get right, zero, one, two or three? Tell me in the comments. Now try it on a friend, and start with the sun.

key_facts: The sun emits light across all visible wavelengths, making its actual color pure white.
Earth's atmosphere scatters shorter wavelengths of light, causing the sun to appear yellow, orange, or red.
Polar bears have completely black skin underneath their fur to absorb and retain heat.
Polar bear cubs are born with pink skin that gradually turns black within several months.
Individual strands of polar bear fur are hollow and translucent, appearing white only due to light scattering.
Baby flamingos hatch with grey or dull white down feathers.
Flamingos develop their distinctive pink color by absorbing carotenoid pigments found in their diet of brine shrimp and algae.

package.title: How Popcorn Pops: 135 PSI Inside One Kernel
package.description:
Why does popcorn pop? Here's how popcorn pops, the popcorn science of steam building up to 135 PSI inside one kernel until the hull bursts.

In this Short: the water and starch inside a kernel, the hull that traps the steam, the 135 PSI pop, and why popcorn jumps.

Sources:
https://www.popcorn.org/All-About-Popcorn/What-Makes-Popcorn-Pop
tags: why does some popcorn not pop
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: a kernel needs about fourteen percent moisture inside to pop well, which is why old, dried-out kernels often don't. What's your favorite popcorn topping?

scenes.text: Before a popcorn kernel pops, the pressure inside builds to about nine times the air around you. Here's why.
scenes.label: 9X PRESSURE
scenes.image_prompt: Extreme macro close-up of golden corn kernels heating on a dark cast iron skillet, subtle heat haze shimmering over the glossy yellow skins, cinematic lighting.

scenes.text: Let's look inside one tiny kernel. Each kernel holds a drop of water and soft starch, inside a tough shell called the hull.
scenes.label: INSIDE A KERNEL
scenes.image_prompt: Stylized 3D scientific cross-section diagram of a single corn kernel revealing translucent moisture droplets embedded within dense white starch, surrounded by a tough golden pericarp hull.

scenes.text: Heat it, and that water turns into steam. But the hull won't let the steam out.
scenes.label: TRAPPED STEAM
scenes.image_prompt: Extreme close-up of a single corn kernel sizzling in hot oil with delicate wisps of steam attempting to escape the hard outer shell, glowing amber backlight.

scenes.text: So the kernel keeps heating, to around three hundred forty-seven degrees Fahrenheit. Inside, the starch turns into a hot, gooey gel.
scenes.label: 347°F
scenes.image_prompt: Visual cutaway illustration of a corn kernel at 347 degrees Fahrenheit, the internal endosperm glowing molten white-gold and turning into a molten gel matrix under immense heat.

scenes.text: The pressure climbs to about one hundred thirty-five pounds per square inch. Then, pop! The hull bursts.
scenes.label: 135 PSI
scenes.image_prompt: High-speed macro photography capturing the precise fraction of a second a popcorn hull cracks open, bright white molten starch erupting violently outward against a dark background.

scenes.text: The starch puffs up and sets into that fluffy shape, up to fifty times bigger.
scenes.label: UP TO 50X BIGGER
scenes.image_prompt: Ultra-slow-motion capture of popped white corn foam solidifying mid-air into an intricate, fluffy cloud shape, glowing under dramatic studio spotlights.

scenes.text: And the jump? The first starch out acts like a tiny leg kicking it up.
scenes.label: THE JUMP
scenes.image_prompt: High-speed freeze-frame shot of an exploding popcorn piece kicking off the metallic pan surface, a starch 'leg' launching it upwards into the air.

scenes.text: So that's why popcorn pops: trapped steam builds pressure until the hull gives way.
scenes.label: STEAM VS HULL
scenes.image_prompt: Overhead shot of freshly popped fluffy white popcorn raining down gently into a ceramic bowl, warm steam lingering in soft ambient light.

scenes.text: What's your favorite popcorn topping? Tell me in the comments. And next time you hear that first pop, think about what happens before it.
scenes.label: THAT FIRST POP
scenes.image_prompt: Slow-motion food commercial shot of golden melted butter and fine salt cascading over a towering bowl of freshly popped popcorn, warm and appetizing.

key_facts: Before popping, pressure inside a popcorn kernel reaches about 9 times atmospheric pressure (135 PSI).
Each kernel contains a small droplet of water surrounded by hard starch inside a tough outer shell called the hull.
Heating turns the trapped water into superheated steam that cannot escape the waterproof hull.
The kernel heats up to approximately 347 degrees Fahrenheit (175 degrees Celsius).
The intense heat turns the internal starch into a gelatinous, molten gel.
At approximately 135 PSI, the hull ruptures violently.
As the pressure drops instantly, the superheated gel inflates into airy foam that solidifies into a fluffy shape up to 50 times its original size.
Popcorn jumps because the initial burst of expanding starch pushes forcefully against the pan like a leg kicking off the ground.

Each kernel holds a drop of water and soft starch, inside a tough shell called the hull. Heat it, and that water turns into steam. But the hull won't let the steam out. So the kernel keeps heating, to around three hundred forty-seven degrees Fahrenheit. Inside, the starch turns into a hot, gooey gel. The pressure climbs to about one hundred thirty-five pounds per square inch. Then, pop! The hull bursts. The starch puffs up and sets into that fluffy shape, up to fifty times bigger. And the jump? The first starch out acts like a tiny leg kicking it up. So that's why popcorn pops: trapped steam builds pressure until the hull gives way. What's your favorite popcorn topping? package.title: Why New Baseballs Get 30 Seconds of Mud
package.description:
Why do umpires rub mud on baseballs? Every new MLB baseball gets baseball rubbing mud for at least thirty seconds, because the shiny new ball is too slick for pitchers to grip.

In this Short: why new baseballs are slippery, what umpires tried before, the 1938 Lena Blackburne rubbing mud from a secret New Jersey riverbank, and why MLB still uses it.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_rubbing_mud
https://mentalfloss.com/article/559416/why-new-jersey-mudhole-contains-baseballs-dirtiest-secret
https://baseballhall.org/discover/lena-blackburne-rubbing-mud-a-secret-of-the-game
tags: why do umpires rub mud on baseballs
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: some NFL teams use the same kind of mud to prep footballs. Have you ever noticed new MLB baseballs look a little brown before the first pitch?

scenes.text: Did you know every Major League baseball gets rubbed with mud before you ever see a pitch? But why?
scenes.label: EVERY BALL GETS MUDDY?
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of a pristine white baseball spinning toward the camera under bright stadium floodlights, vertical format 9:16, cinematic sports photography.

scenes.text: Here's the mud, and where it comes from. New baseballs are shiny and slippery, like a wet bar of soap. Pitchers can't grip that gloss.
scenes.label: SHINY = SLIPPERY
scenes.image_prompt: Studio macro shot of a glossy, reflective brand-new white leather baseball sitting under dramatic studio lighting showing smooth slick texture, vertical 9:16.

scenes.text: So every ball has to be rubbed until the shine is gone. People once tried tobacco juice, shoe polish, even bleacher dirt.
scenes.label: RULE: GLOSS OFF
scenes.image_prompt: Vintage retro 1930s baseball dugout bench with weathered leather baseball gloves, a wooden bat, and jars of dark shoe polish and dirt, sepia toned, vertical 9:16.

scenes.text: Then, in nineteen thirty-eight, a coach named Lena Blackburne found a special mud near a New Jersey river.
scenes.label: SECRET MUD
scenes.image_prompt: A quiet misty riverbank along a secluded New Jersey waterway with thick dark silky mud on the shore surrounded by tall reeds, vertical 9:16 atmospheric photography.

scenes.text: It's said to feel like chocolate pudding and cold cream. The exact spot is still a secret.
scenes.label: LOCATION: SECRET
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of hands rubbing rich ultra-fine dark brown river mud between fingers, creamy and smooth texture like pudding, macro detail, vertical 9:16.

scenes.text: Each team gets about ten pounds a season, and every ball gets at least thirty seconds of rubbing.
scenes.label: 10 LBS PER TEAM
scenes.image_prompt: Close-up of an equipment manager's hands firmly rubbing dark river mud onto a new white baseball, turning the leather dull and tacky, vertical 9:16.

scenes.text: That's why: the mud gives pitchers grip, and nothing's replaced it yet.
scenes.label: GRIP WINS
scenes.image_prompt: A Major League pitcher on the mound in mid-throw, fingers gripping tightly onto the red seams of a dull mud-rubbed baseball, vertical 9:16 dynamic action shot.

scenes.text: Would you trust the mud, or invent something better? Tell me in the comments. And next time you watch a pitch, remember that ball got muddy first.
scenes.label: WATCH THE NEXT PITCH
scenes.image_prompt: Slow-motion action perspective of a baseball crossing home plate past an out-of-focus batter, stadium lights glowing in the evening air, vertical 9:16.

key_facts: Every Major League baseball is rubbed with mud before game use to remove slickness.
Brand new factory baseballs have a glossy, slippery sheen that makes them hard for pitchers to grip.
Early teams experimented with tobacco juice, shoe polish, and bleacher dirt to dull the shine.
In 1938, coach Lena Blackburne discovered a unique silt mud along a New Jersey riverbank that perfected the process.
The mud is uniquely fine and described as feeling like chocolate pudding and cold cream.
The exact geographic location where the mud is harvested remains a closely guarded secret.
Each MLB club receives roughly 10 pounds of the mud per season.
Each individual game ball is rubbed for at least 30 seconds before use.

In the UK, 'pants' refers exclusively to underwear, while outerwear for legs is termed 'trousers'.

scenes.text: At number two, flamingos. Balanced on pencil-thin legs, their vicious territorial squabbles are basically just aggressive, tangled-neck pool noodle fights.

scenes.text: And at number one, three-toed sloths. Fighting over mates in literal slow motion, one single dramatic hook takes about ten business days to land.

scenes.text: Honestly, even a sleeping snail could dodge it. Which of these hilarious fighters would you hire as your personal bodyguard?

Flamingos resolve disputes using beak jabs and neck fencing while balancing on one or two legs.
Three-toed sloths fight rivals in canopy trees using deliberate, very slow claw swiping motions.

package.description:
These are five real places that look photoshopped: Lake Hillier the pink lake, Caño Cristales the river of five colors, the Giant's Causeway, the Zhangye rainbow mountains and Salar de Uyuni, the salt flat mirror. They look fake, but every one is a real place on Earth.

In this Short: why each place looks unreal, counting down to the salt flat that turns into a mirror.

key_facts: All five featured locations are real, natural landscapes open to visitors.
Giant's Causeway in Northern Ireland consists of approximately 40,000 predominantly hexagonal basalt columns formed by cooling volcanic lava.
Zhangye Danxia in China gets its rainbow-striped mountains from layered mineral deposits like iron oxide laid down over millions of years.
Lake Hillier in Australia maintains a permanent bubble-gum pink color caused primarily by salt-loving microalgae, remaining pink even when placed in a glass.
Caño Cristales in Colombia becomes the 'river of five colors' when the endemic aquatic plant Macarenia clavigera blooms bright red under specific light and water conditions.
Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat on Earth.
Seasonal rainwater over Salar de Uyuni forms an expansive, ultra-thin sheet of water that creates the world's largest natural mirror.

package.title: The Space Signal Heard Once in 1977
package.description:
The true story of the Wow signal, the 1977 space signal picked up for 72 seconds by Ohio's Big Ear radio telescope and never heard again. An astronomer circled it on the printout and wrote Wow.

In this Short: what the Wow signal was, why it lasted 72 seconds, what 6EQUJ5 means, and the 2024 idea that might explain it.

This is a true story.

key_facts: On August 15, 1977, the Big Ear radio telescope in Ohio detected a strong narrowband radio signal.
Big Ear was a fixed telescope that used Earth's rotation to sweep across the sky.
The signal originated from the constellation Sagittarius and lasted for 72 seconds, matching the telescope's window of observation for a celestial point source.
The alphanumeric sequence 6EQUJ5 represented signal intensity, where letters corresponded to values exceeding 9.
Astronomer Jerry Ehman discovered the signal on computer printouts, circled it in red pen, and wrote 'Wow!'.
Subsequent searches by multiple radio telescopes failed to detect a repeat signal.
In 2024, researchers proposed that a rare magnetar flare exciting an interstellar hydrogen cloud could potentially explain the emission.
package.script: You could listen to the sky for almost fifty years and never hear it again, but in nineteen seventy-seven, Ohio's Big Ear did. This is the true story of the Wow signal. August fifteenth, nineteen seventy-seven. Big Ear, a radio telescope, is scanning space. It didn't move. Earth's spin swept the sky past it. It caught a strong, sharp signal from the direction of Sagittarius. It lasted seventy-two seconds, exactly as long as one spot of sky stays in view. The printout showed a strange code: six, E, Q, U, J, five. Letters meant extra strong. An astronomer circled it in red ink and wrote: Wow. Telescopes went back again and again. Nothing. In twenty twenty-four, scientists suggested a magnetar flare may have made a hydrogen cloud flash. It's still just an idea. So that's the Wow signal: seventy-two seconds, one word, no repeat. Nature, or something else? Tell me in the comments. Because we're still listening, and so far, nothing.

key_facts: Movie theaters use Flavacol, a fine salt containing artificial butter flavor and yellow food dyes, to season popcorn.

package.title: How Desert Ice Houses Worked 2,400 Years Ago
package.description:
How did ancient people make ice in the desert without electricity? A yakhchal was an ancient Persian ice house: shaded pools froze on clear winter nights, and a giant thick-walled cone stored the ice all summer.

In this Short: the shade wall, the night-sky freezing trick, and how the cone kept ice cold through a desert summer.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakhch%C4%81l
https://www.birdsoutsidemywindow.org/2021/01/06/how-to-make-ice-in-the-desert/
https://www.historicmysteries.com/yakhchal/
tags: how did ancient people make ice
package.pinned_comment: Bonus fact: the walls were made of a special mortar mixed with sand, clay, lime, ash, egg whites and even goat hair. What ancient invention should we animate next?

scenes.text: How did people make ice in the desert, long before freezers?
scenes.image_prompt: 3D animated wide shot of a sun-baked clay-colored desert at noon with heat shimmer, featuring a tall cone-shaped mudbrick building and an adjoining long adobe wall under a bright sky, stylized clean render

scenes.text: In ancient Persia, water flowed from underground channels into shallow pools.
scenes.image_prompt: 3D cutaway cross-section of desert ground showing an underground stone aqueduct channel flowing upward into long shallow rectangular reflection pools adjacent to a tall mudbrick wall
scenes.shot: 3D cross-section cutaway of the ground: a narrow underground tunnel carries water up into long shallow pools that sit beside the tall wall, camera tracks along the flowing water

scenes.text: A tall wall kept those pools in shade.

package.title: Top 5 Animal Dads (#1 Gets Pregnant)
package.description:
These animal dads do all the work, from the male seahorse that gives birth to the emperor penguin that goes up to 67 days without eating. Here are the best animal fathers in nature, counted down from five to one.

In this Short: the giant water bug, the smooth guardian frog, the greater rhea, the emperor penguin and the seahorse.

package.title: The 131-Year-Old Message in a Bottle 🍾
package.description:
The oldest message in a bottle ever found was thrown from the German ship Paula in 1886 and found on a beach in Western Australia in 2018. This message in a bottle spent 131 years lost before anyone read it.

In this Short: how the bottle was found, what the note said, and why German captains threw thousands of bottles into the sea.

This is a true story.

Sources:

https://wgbh.org/news/2018-03-07/oldest-known-message-in-a-bottle-found-in-australia
